title: Knee, Leg, Ankle & Foot
summary: Explore the joints and compartments that turn the lower limb into a stable but adaptable walking machine.

lessons.title: Knee Joint: Menisci, Cruciate & Collateral Ligaments

levels.kid:
Your knee is like a door hinge, but smarter. It bends and straightens so you can walk, jump and kick a ball.

Two big bones meet at the knee: the thigh bone on top and the shin bone below. Their ends are round and fairly flat, so they don't fit together tightly on their own.

So the knee has helpers:
- Two rubbery C-shaped cushions called **menisci**. They work like a soft cup that holds the round bone and soaks up bumps.
- Strong straps called **ligaments**. Two cross inside the knee in an X. Two more run down the sides like guard rails.

Athletes sometimes tear these straps when they twist or stop suddenly. Doctors can test them and help them heal.
levels.hs:
The **knee** is the largest joint in the body. It is a **synovial joint**, meaning it is surrounded by a capsule filled with slippery fluid. The femur (thigh bone) sits on the flat top of the tibia (shin bone), and the patella (kneecap) glides in a groove at the front. The bone shapes give little stability, so soft tissues do most of the work.

**Menisci** are two C-shaped wedges of **fibrocartilage** sitting on the tibia:
- The **medial meniscus** (inner side) is C-shaped and firmly attached, so it tears more often.
- The **lateral meniscus** (outer side) is more O-shaped and more mobile.
They spread load, absorb shock and deepen the socket.

**Cruciate ligaments** (from Latin for "cross") sit inside the knee and form an X:
- **Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL)**: stops the tibia sliding forward.
- **Posterior cruciate ligament (PCL)**: stops the tibia sliding backward.

**Collateral ligaments** run down the sides:
- **Medial collateral ligament (MCL)**: resists the knee being pushed inward.
- **Lateral collateral ligament (LCL)**: resists the knee being pushed outward.

Real example: a soccer player plants a foot, twists and lands awkwardly. They hear a "pop" and the knee swells within hours. This is a classic **ACL tear**, often with meniscus or MCL damage too.
levels.college:
The knee consists of the **tibiofemoral** joints (medial and lateral) and the **patellofemoral** joint, all inside one synovial cavity. It is a modified hinge: mainly flexion and extension, with some rotation when the knee is flexed.

**Menisci**
- Their outer rim attaches to the capsule. Their horns anchor to the intercondylar area of the tibia.
- The **medial meniscus** is attached to the deep fibers of the MCL and the capsule, so it is less mobile and injured more often.
- The **lateral meniscus** is separated from the LCL by the popliteus tendon. Popliteus also pulls it backward during flexion, so it moves more.
- Blood supply comes from the genicular arteries and reaches only the outer third (the **red zone**). The inner white zone heals poorly.

**Cruciate ligaments** lie inside the capsule but outside the synovial lining.
- **ACL**: runs from the anterior intercondylar tibia up and back to the medial surface of the lateral femoral condyle. It resists anterior tibial translation and internal rotation. Tested with the **anterior drawer** and **Lachman** tests.
- **PCL**: runs from the posterior intercondylar tibia up and forward to the lateral surface of the medial femoral condyle. It is stronger and resists posterior translation. Tested with the **posterior drawer** test; injured in "dashboard" impacts.

**Collateral ligaments**
- **MCL** (tibial collateral): a broad band attached to the medial meniscus. It resists **valgus** stress (knee pushed inward).
- **LCL** (fibular collateral): a cord-like band to the fibular head, separate from the meniscus. It resists **varus** stress.

**Locking and unlocking**: in the last degrees of extension the femur rotates medially on the fixed tibia (the **screw-home mechanism**), tightening the ligaments. **Popliteus** unlocks the knee to start flexion.

The **unhappy triad** (ACL, MCL, medial meniscus) follows a lateral blow to a planted, extended knee. Lateral meniscus tears are actually common with acute ACL tears.
levels.phd:
Knee stability comes from a layered system: static restraints (ligaments, menisci, capsule), the shape of the joint surfaces, and dynamic restraint from muscles.

**Meniscal biomechanics.** Meniscal collagen runs mostly in a **circumferential** direction, with radial "tie" fibers. When load presses the femur down, the wedge tries to squeeze outward. The circumferential fibers resist this as **hoop stress**, turning compression into tension. That is why a complete **radial tear** or **root avulsion** destroys function: without an intact ring and anchored horns, there is no hoop tension. Under load the menisci carry roughly half of the load in extension and more in flexion. Fairbank (1948) described the narrowing and ridging seen on X-ray after total meniscectomy, which first showed their protective role.

**ACL microanatomy.** The ACL has two functional bundles named for where they attach on the tibia. The **anteromedial bundle** is tight in flexion. The **posterolateral bundle** is tight near extension and controls rotation. The ACL carries proprioceptive mechanoreceptors (Ruffini and Pacinian endings), so rupture also impairs sensorimotor control. The PCL is similarly described as an anterolateral bundle, dominant in flexion, and a posteromedial bundle. The meniscofemoral ligaments of **Humphrey** (in front of the PCL) and **Wrisberg** (behind it) link the lateral meniscus's posterior horn to the medial femoral condyle.

**Kinematics.** The knee does not roll like a simple hinge. The lateral femoral condyle rolls back more than the medial one during flexion, coupling flexion with tibial internal rotation. The cruciates form a crossed **four-bar linkage** that guides this roll-and-glide.

**Posterolateral corner (PLC).** The LCL, popliteus tendon and **popliteofibular ligament** resist varus and external rotation. Missed PLC injuries are a recognized cause of ACL reconstruction failure.

**Controversy.** Claes et al. (2013) described an **anterolateral ligament (ALL)** linked to Segond fractures. Its existence as a distinct ligament versus a capsular thickening is still debated, but it renewed interest in anterolateral rotational control.
levels.expert:
Clinically, the biggest knee decisions depend on timing, the pattern of injury, and protecting the joint over the long term.

**Examination pearls.** **Lachman** at 20-30 degrees of flexion is the most sensitive office test for ACL rupture. The anterior drawer can look falsely normal when hamstring guarding or the meniscal posterior horn blocks movement. The **pivot shift** best matches patient-reported instability but needs a relaxed patient, often under anesthesia. For the PCL, look for **posterior sag** first; a sagging tibia can create a falsely positive anterior drawer. A positive **dial test** at 30 degrees only suggests a PLC injury; positive at both 30 and 90 degrees suggests PLC plus PCL. Valgus laxity in full extension (not just at 30 degrees) implies cruciate or posteromedial damage beyond an isolated MCL injury.

**Imaging signs.** On MRI, **bone bruises** on the lateral femoral condyle and posterolateral tibial plateau are typical of ACL pivot injury. A **Segond fracture** (small avulsion from the lateral tibial plateau) is nearly diagnostic of ACL tear. Look specifically for **ramp lesions** (meniscocapsular separation at the posterior horn of the medial meniscus) and posterior root tears, which are often missed.

**Management trends.**
- Isolated MCL tears usually heal without surgery, thanks to their blood supply and broad attachments.
- ACL reconstruction graft choices include bone-patellar tendon-bone, hamstring and quadriceps tendon. In young pivoting athletes, adding a **lateral extra-articular tenodesis** lowered graft failure in the STABILITY trial (Getgood et al., 2020).
- The KANON trial showed that rehab with optional delayed reconstruction gave similar 2- and 5-year outcomes to early reconstruction in active adults, so not every patient needs surgery.
- Meniscus care has moved toward **repair over resection**. Root repair restores hoop function. Arthroscopic partial meniscectomy for degenerative tears performed no better than sham surgery in the FIDELITY trial.

**Open questions.** Post-traumatic osteoarthritis develops in many patients within 10-20 years even after successful reconstruction, which suggests the damage at injury (cartilage and biology) matters as much as the remaining laxity. Bridge-enhanced ACL repair and biologic augmentation are under study but not yet standard.

keyPoints: The knee relies on soft tissues more than bone shape for stability
Menisci are C-shaped fibrocartilage wedges that spread load via hoop stress
The medial meniscus is less mobile and tears more often than the lateral
ACL resists forward tibial slide; PCL resists backward slide
MCL resists valgus stress; LCL resists varus stress
Screw-home locks the extended knee; popliteus unlocks it

test.q: What type of tissue forms the menisci?
test.explain: Menisci are fibrocartilage wedges. Hyaline cartilage covers the joint surfaces of the bones.

test.q: Why is the medial meniscus injured more often than the lateral meniscus?
choices: It is pulled backward by popliteus
It is attached to the MCL and less mobile
It has no blood supply at its rim
It is shaped more like a closed ring
test.explain: The medial meniscus is tethered to the MCL and capsule, so it can't move out of the way. Popliteus moves the lateral meniscus.

test.q: The anterior cruciate ligament mainly prevents the tibia from:
test.explain: The ACL resists anterior tibial translation. The PCL resists posterior translation.

test.q: A blow to the outer side of the knee creates valgus stress. Which ligament resists it?
test.explain: Valgus stress pushes the knee inward and stretches the medial side, so the MCL resists it.

test.q: Which test is described as the most sensitive office test for an ACL tear?
test.explain: Lachman is done at 20-30 degrees of flexion and is highly sensitive for ACL rupture.

test.q: The classic (O'Donoghue) 'unhappy triad' involves the ACL, the MCL and the:
test.explain: O'Donoghue described the classic triad as ACL, MCL and medial meniscus injury, from a lateral (valgus) blow to a planted, flexed knee. Later studies of acute injuries found lateral meniscus tears more often, but the classic definition names the medial meniscus.

test.q: Which muscle unlocks the fully extended knee to begin flexion?
test.explain: Popliteus rotates the femur laterally on the tibia, reversing the screw-home lock.

test.q: Why does the inner 'white zone' of a meniscus heal poorly?
choices: It is covered by synovial fluid
It bears little load during walking
It lacks a good blood supply
test.explain: Genicular arteries reach only the outer third (red zone), so inner tears have little healing capacity.

test.q: A front-seat passenger's knee hits the dashboard. Which ligament is classically torn?
test.explain: The impact pushes the tibia backward, which the PCL normally resists.

test.q: The lateral collateral ligament attaches below to the head of the ___.
test.explain: The LCL (fibular collateral ligament) runs from the lateral femoral epicondyle to the fibular head.

test.q: What is the name of the mechanism in which the femur rotates medially in the last degrees of extension to lock the knee?
test.explain: The screw-home mechanism tightens ligaments for a stable standing knee.

test.q: The word cruciate comes from Latin for ___, because the two ligaments form an X.
test.explain: The ACL and PCL cross each other inside the knee.

kidTest.q: What are the menisci in the knee?
choices: Small, flat bones that sit behind the kneecap
Rubbery cartilage pads between the bones
Tiny muscles that help bend and straighten the knee
kidTest.explain: Menisci are C-shaped cartilage cushions between the thigh and shin bones that soak up bumps.

kidTest.q: Which two big bones meet at the knee?
kidTest.explain: The thigh bone sits on top of the shin bone.

kidTest.q: What shape do the two inside ligaments make?
kidTest.explain: The cruciate ligaments cross like an X.

kidTest.q: How do athletes often hurt knee ligaments?
kidTest.explain: Sudden twists and stops can tear the straps.

kidTest.q: The strong straps holding the knee are called l _ _ _ _ _ _ _ s.
kidTest.explain: Ligaments are tough straps that hold bones together.

advancedTest.q: Why does a complete radial tear or root avulsion ruin meniscal function even if most tissue remains?
choices: It cuts the genicular blood supply to the outer red zone
It breaks the circumferential ring that generates hoop tension
It detaches the meniscus from the medial collateral ligament
It destroys the proprioceptive endings within the meniscal horns
advancedTest.explain: Load is converted into circumferential hoop stress; without a continuous anchored ring, the meniscus extrudes and stops sharing load.

advancedTest.q: A patient has a positive anterior drawer, but the tibia sags backward at rest. What is the likely explanation?
choices: The posterolateral corner is intact and over-tightened
The ACL is torn and the menisci block posterior motion
The tibia starts posteriorly, so a PCL tear mimics ACL laxity
Hamstring guarding exaggerates forward motion of the tibia
advancedTest.explain: With a PCL tear the tibia sags back; pulling it forward to neutral looks like an anterior drawer.

advancedTest.q: A dial test is positive at both 30 and 90 degrees of flexion. This best suggests:
choices: Combined PCL and posterolateral corner injury
Combined ACL and medial meniscus injury
advancedTest.explain: PLC injury alone shows at 30 degrees; added laxity at 90 degrees implies PCL involvement.

advancedTest.q: Many patients develop osteoarthritis years after a successful ACL reconstruction. What does this most suggest?
choices: Rehabilitation without surgery reliably prevents arthritis
Graft choice is the main determinant of arthritis risk
Damage at the time of injury matters beyond residual laxity
Reconstruction itself is the direct cause of the arthritis
advancedTest.explain: Restoring stability doesn't prevent OA, implying cartilage and biological injury at the time of trauma drive it.

lessons.title: The Popliteal Fossa

levels.kid:
Bend your knee and feel the soft hollow at the back. That hollow is called the **popliteal fossa**. It is like a hidden hallway where important things pass from your thigh down to your leg.

In this hallway there are three big travellers. A **nerve** carries messages, like a phone wire. A **vein** carries blood back to your heart. An **artery** carries fresh blood down to your foot. The artery sits deepest, closest to the bone, where it is safest.

Strong muscles make the walls of the hallway, like the sides of a diamond. Doctors can press gently in this hollow to feel your pulse beating. Because so many important things live here, doctors are very careful when they fix knees.
levels.hs:
The **popliteal fossa** is the diamond-shaped space behind the knee. ("Popliteal" comes from the Latin word for the ham of the leg.) It acts as a passageway that carries nerves and blood vessels between the thigh and the leg.

Its four borders are muscles:
- **Upper outer (superolateral)**: biceps femoris, one of the hamstrings.
- **Upper inner (superomedial)**: semimembranosus and semitendinosus.
- **Lower borders**: the two heads of **gastrocnemius**, the main calf muscle.

The roof is skin and a tough sheet of fascia. The floor is the back of the femur, the knee joint capsule, and the popliteus muscle.

Contents, from the surface to the deepest layer:
- **Tibial nerve**, the most superficial of the main structures.
- **Popliteal vein**, in the middle.
- **Popliteal artery**, the deepest, lying against the bone.

The **common fibular (peroneal) nerve** runs along the outer edge beside biceps femoris. The fossa also holds fat and **popliteal lymph nodes**.

One real example is the **Baker's cyst**, a fluid-filled swelling behind the knee. It often forms when a bursa linked to the knee joint fills up, usually in people with arthritis or a meniscus tear. Doctors also feel the **popliteal pulse** here. Because the artery is so deep, the knee is usually bent slightly to relax the fascia before pressing in.
levels.college:
The **popliteal fossa** is a diamond-shaped intermuscular space posterior to the knee. It is the main conduit for neurovascular structures passing between the thigh and the leg.

**Boundaries**
- Superolateral: biceps femoris.
- Superomedial: semimembranosus, with semitendinosus lying over it.
- Inferolateral: lateral head of gastrocnemius, plus plantaris.
- Inferomedial: medial head of gastrocnemius.
- Roof: skin, superficial fascia carrying the **small saphenous vein** and the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve, and the **popliteal fascia** (a continuation of the fascia lata).
- Floor, superior to inferior: the popliteal surface of the femur, the **oblique popliteal ligament** (an expansion of the semimembranosus tendon), and the fascia over popliteus.

**Contents, superficial to deep:** tibial nerve, popliteal vein, popliteal artery. The artery and vein share a tight fibrous sheath.
- The **sciatic nerve** usually divides at the apex of the fossa. The **tibial nerve** descends in the midline. The **common fibular nerve** follows the medial edge of biceps femoris and then winds around the fibular neck.
- The **popliteal artery** continues from the femoral artery at the **adductor hiatus**. It gives off five **genicular arteries** to the knee anastomosis and sural branches to gastrocnemius. At the lower border of popliteus it divides into the anterior and posterior tibial arteries.
- The **small saphenous vein** pierces the deep fascia and drains into the popliteal vein.
- **Popliteal lymph nodes** (about six) drain lymph that travels with the small saphenous vein. Their efferents run to the deep inguinal nodes.

**Clinical points**
- The pulse is best felt with the knee flexed, which relaxes the fascia.
- **Popliteal artery aneurysm** is the most common peripheral arterial aneurysm.
- A **Baker's cyst** usually arises from the gastrocnemius-semimembranosus bursa, which communicates with the knee joint.
- A fracture of the distal femur can injure the artery. The gastrocnemius pulls the distal fragment backward toward the vessel.
levels.phd:
The popliteal fossa is a bottleneck. Every major neurovascular structure of the leg passes through a narrow space bounded by bone and the hamstring and gastrocnemius muscles, and the space is partly tethered at both ends. This anatomical fixation explains much of its pathology.

**Vascular fixation and injury.** The popliteal artery is anchored proximally at the adductor hiatus and distally beneath the **soleal arch** (tendinous arch of soleus). Between these points it lies against the femur and the posterior capsule. In **knee dislocation**, the artery cannot move away and is stretched or torn. Large series report arterial injury in roughly a fifth to a third of dislocations, and the risk is highest with posterior dislocation. The **genicular anastomosis** (superior and inferior medial and lateral genicular arteries, the middle genicular, and the descending genicular from the femoral) cannot supply the leg alone after acute occlusion. Ischaemia lasting more than about 6-8 hours carries a high amputation rate.

**Developmental variants.** The popliteal artery comes from the embryonic axial (sciatic) artery and later remodelling. **Popliteal artery entrapment syndrome (PAES)** results from an abnormal relationship with the medial head of gastrocnemius, which forms during its migration from lateral to medial. In the Rich/Love-Whelan/Insua classification, types I-IV are anatomical variants, type V includes the vein, and type VI is **functional entrapment** by a hypertrophied but normally placed muscle. Branching variants also matter. A **high division** above popliteus, or a trifurcation, occurs in a few percent of limbs.

**Neural anatomy.** The sciatic nerve is two separately wrapped trunks in one sheath, the tibial and the common fibular. Their separation level ranges from the pelvis to the fossa apex, and the level is usually near the apex of the fossa. The fibular component has fewer and larger fascicles, less connective tissue, and is tethered at the fibular head. These features fit its greater vulnerability to stretch compared with the tibial component.

**Cysts.** Baker's cysts form through a valve-like opening between the joint and the gastrocnemius-semimembranosus bursa. Fluid can enter the bursa on flexion but returns poorly. Rupture can track into the calf and mimic **deep vein thrombosis**, which is the classic "pseudothrombophlebitis".
levels.expert:
Clinically, the popliteal fossa is unforgiving because a missed vascular lesion becomes visible only when it is already late.

**Knee dislocation workup.** Up to about half of dislocations reduce on their own before the patient arrives, so a normal-looking knee does not exclude arterial injury. Current practice relies on serial pulse examination plus the **ankle-brachial index (ABI)**. An ABI below 0.9 prompts CT angiography. An ABI of 0.9 or above with normal pulses supports serial observation, an approach validated by Mills and colleagues. Hard signs (pulsatile bleeding, expanding haematoma, absent pulses, a cold limb) mean going straight to the operating theatre. After revascularisation, consider prophylactic **four-compartment fasciotomy**, because reperfusion oedema can cause compartment syndrome.

**Surgical approaches.** The posterior approach uses a lazy-S incision that crosses the flexion crease obliquely so that the scar does not contract. It runs between the heads of gastrocnemius, and the medial sural cutaneous nerve and small saphenous vein act as guides to the deeper neurovascular bundle. The tibial nerve is met first, then the vein, then the artery. The posterior cruciate ligament is reached through a posteromedial window, often in prone position. The medial approach is preferred for vascular bypass.

**Iatrogenic pitfalls.** All-inside meniscal repair devices and posterior drilling for anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction can reach the popliteal artery. With the knee flexed to 90°, the artery falls back several millimetres from the tibia, so many procedures are done in flexion. Neurosurgeons and orthopaedic surgeons decompressing the common fibular nerve at the fibular neck should trace it back to the lateral border of the fossa to confirm continuity and find a high bifurcation.

**Imaging and diagnosis.** On ultrasound, a Baker's cyst shows a characteristic "neck" between semimembranosus and the medial gastrocnemius. This neck distinguishes it from a popliteal aneurysm, which pulsates and may contain thrombus. **Popliteal aneurysms** are bilateral in about half of patients and often accompany abdominal aortic aneurysm, so screening of the other knee and the aorta is warranted. Their main danger is distal embolisation and thrombosis rather than rupture.

**Open questions.** Functional PAES in athletes is hard to separate from normal compression during provocative manoeuvres. Some asymptomatic people show occlusion when tested in plantarflexion, so the threshold for surgery remains debated. Recent provocative MR angiography and dynamic ultrasound protocols aim to standardise the diagnosis.

keyPoints: The popliteal fossa is a diamond-shaped space behind the knee
Borders: biceps femoris, semimembranosus/semitendinosus, and both heads of gastrocnemius
Contents superficial to deep: tibial nerve, popliteal vein, popliteal artery
Common fibular nerve runs along biceps femoris toward the fibular neck
Popliteal artery is tethered and at high risk in knee dislocation
Baker's cysts arise from the gastrocnemius-semimembranosus bursa

test.q: Which muscle forms the superolateral border of the popliteal fossa?
test.explain: Biceps femoris forms the upper outer border. Semimembranosus forms the upper inner border.

test.q: Which structures form the two inferior borders of the fossa?
test.explain: The medial and lateral heads of gastrocnemius form the lower borders.

test.q: Which is the deepest of the main structures in the popliteal fossa?
test.explain: From superficial to deep, the order is tibial nerve, popliteal vein, popliteal artery. The artery lies against the femur.

test.q: The popliteal artery is a continuation of the femoral artery at the:
test.explain: The femoral artery passes through the adductor hiatus and becomes the popliteal artery.

test.q: Which nerve runs along the edge of biceps femoris and winds around the fibular neck?
test.explain: The common fibular (peroneal) nerve follows the medial border of biceps femoris and then winds around the fibular neck. The tibial nerve stays in the midline of the popliteal fossa.

test.q: Why is the knee flexed when checking the popliteal pulse?
choices: It squeezes the tibial nerve aside
It speeds up the blood flow
It moves the artery to the surface
test.explain: Flexion relaxes the tight roof fascia, which lets the fingers press deep enough to feel the artery.

test.q: A Baker's cyst most often arises from which bursa?
test.explain: The gastrocnemius-semimembranosus bursa communicates with the knee joint and can fill with joint fluid. The other bursae lie at the front of the knee.

test.q: Which vein pierces the roof of the fossa to join the popliteal vein?
test.explain: The small saphenous vein drains into the popliteal vein. The great saphenous vein runs on the medial side of the leg.

test.q: The popliteal artery ends by dividing into the:
test.explain: At the lower border of popliteus it divides into the anterior and posterior tibial arteries.

test.q: Which nerve is the most superficial of the main structures in the popliteal fossa?
test.explain: The tibial nerve lies most superficial, then the vein, then the artery.

test.q: The arteries that supply the knee anastomosis are called the ___ arteries.
test.explain: The popliteal artery gives off five genicular arteries to the knee.

test.q: The large nerve that usually divides at the apex of the fossa is the ___ nerve.
test.explain: The sciatic nerve splits into the tibial and common fibular nerves.

kidTest.q: Where is the popliteal fossa?
kidTest.explain: It is the soft hollow at the back of the knee.

kidTest.q: What does an artery carry?
kidTest.explain: The artery carries fresh blood down to the foot.

kidTest.q: Which traveller sits deepest, close to the bone?
kidTest.explain: The artery sits deepest, where it is safest.

kidTest.q: What makes the walls of the hollow?
kidTest.explain: Muscles form the sides of the diamond.

kidTest.q: Which traveller works like a phone wire carrying messages? n _ _ _ _
kidTest.explain: A nerve carries messages, like a phone wire.

advancedTest.q: Why is the popliteal artery especially vulnerable in knee dislocation?
choices: It is the most superficial structure in the fossa
It is tethered at the adductor hiatus and soleal arch
It lacks any collateral genicular branches
It runs lateral to the common fibular nerve
advancedTest.explain: Fixation at both ends stops the artery from moving out of the way, so it is stretched or torn. It is deep, not superficial, and it does have collaterals, though they are not enough.

advancedTest.q: A patient's dislocated knee has reduced on its own, the pulses feel present, and the ABI is 0.8. Best next step?
choices: Repeat the pulse check in a week
advancedTest.explain: An ABI below 0.9 suggests arterial injury and warrants CT angiography, even when pulses seem present.

advancedTest.q: Type VI popliteal artery entrapment differs from types I-IV because it involves:
choices: A hypertrophied but normally placed muscle
Compression of the popliteal vein instead
An abnormal origin of the artery itself
advancedTest.explain: Type VI is functional entrapment by muscle bulk, with no anatomical malposition. Types I-IV involve abnormal anatomy.

advancedTest.q: After finding a popliteal aneurysm, which further check is most justified?
choices: Biopsy of the popliteal lymph nodes
Imaging of the opposite knee and aorta
Nerve conduction study of the tibial nerve
advancedTest.explain: Popliteal aneurysms are bilateral in about half of patients and are often linked to abdominal aortic aneurysm.

lessons.title: Leg Compartments: Anterior, Lateral & Posterior

levels.kid:
Your lower leg, between your knee and your ankle, is packed like a suitcase with separate pockets. Tough sheets of tissue split it into rooms called **compartments**.

Each room holds a team of muscles with its own nerve, like a team with its own coach.
- The **front** team lifts your toes up, so you don't trip.
- The **side** team tips your foot outward and helps you balance.
- The **back** team is the strongest. It pushes you up onto your tiptoes to jump and run.

The walls are very tough and don't stretch much. If a room swells after a bad injury, the muscles get squeezed. Doctors watch for this carefully, because squeezed muscles need help quickly.
levels.hs:
The leg (anatomists use "leg" for knee to ankle) has two bones, the **tibia** and the **fibula**. They are joined by a sheet called the **interosseous membrane**. Strong fascia (connective tissue) walls called **intermuscular septa** split the leg into **compartments**. Each compartment holds muscles that share a job, a nerve and a blood supply.

- **Anterior compartment**: tibialis anterior, extensor digitorum longus, extensor hallucis longus, fibularis tertius. These muscles **dorsiflex** the foot (pull the toes up). Nerve: **deep fibular (peroneal) nerve**.
- **Lateral compartment**: fibularis longus and brevis. They **evert** the foot (turn the sole outward). Nerve: **superficial fibular nerve**.
- **Posterior compartment**: gastrocnemius, soleus and deeper muscles. They **plantarflex** the foot (point the toes) and invert it. Nerve: **tibial nerve**.

The deep fascia around the leg is tight and doesn't stretch. After a tibial fracture, bleeding and swelling can raise the pressure inside a compartment until blood can't flow in. This is **acute compartment syndrome**, a surgical emergency. The classic early warning sign is pain far worse than expected, especially when the muscles are passively stretched. Surgeons treat it with **fasciotomy**, cutting the fascia open to release the pressure.

Real example: someone who can't lift the front of the foot after a knee injury may have damaged the common fibular nerve. They develop **foot drop** and walk with a high-stepping gait.
levels.college:
**Boundaries.** The crural fascia wraps the leg and attaches to the anterior and medial borders of the tibia. The anterior and posterior intermuscular septa run to the fibula, and the interosseous membrane links tibia and fibula. Together these create anterior, lateral and posterior compartments. The **transverse intermuscular septum** splits the posterior compartment into superficial and deep parts, giving four functional compartments in total.

**Anterior (dorsiflexors).** Tibialis anterior (also inverts), extensor hallucis longus, extensor digitorum longus and fibularis tertius. Nerve: **deep fibular nerve**. Vessels: **anterior tibial artery**, which passes forward above the interosseous membrane and continues as the dorsalis pedis artery.

**Lateral (evertors).** Fibularis longus and fibularis brevis. Nerve: **superficial fibular nerve**. No major artery runs here; branches of the fibular artery supply it. Fibularis longus crosses the sole to insert on the medial cuneiform and first metatarsal base.

**Superficial posterior.** Gastrocnemius, soleus and plantaris insert by the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon. They are powerful plantarflexors. Gastrocnemius crosses the knee as well, so it also flexes the knee.

**Deep posterior.** Popliteus, flexor hallucis longus, flexor digitorum longus and tibialis posterior (a key inverter). Nerve: **tibial nerve**. Vessels: **posterior tibial artery** and its **fibular branch**.

**Nerve injury patterns:**
- Common fibular nerve (exposed at the fibular neck) causes foot drop, weak eversion and numbness over the dorsum of the foot.
- Deep fibular nerve alone causes foot drop plus numbness of the first web space.
- Tibial nerve injury causes loss of plantarflexion and toe flexion, with sole numbness.

**Compartment syndrome.** Rising pressure inside a closed space first collapses low-pressure veins, then cuts off capillary flow, causing ischemia. The anterior compartment is involved most often. Typical features are pain out of proportion to the injury and pain on passive stretch (plantarflexing the foot stretches the anterior muscles). Paresthesia, paralysis and pulselessness are late signs.
levels.phd:
**Pathophysiology of compartment syndrome.** Matsen's arteriovenous gradient model explains the mechanism. Local blood flow depends on (Pa − Pv)/R. As compartment pressure rises, venous pressure must rise with it to keep veins open, so the gradient falls. Capillary perfusion fails while the large arteries are still patent. This is why distal pulses are usually still present when muscle is already ischemic. Skeletal muscle tolerates roughly 4 hours of warm ischemia with reversible changes. By about 6 hours injury is substantial, and by about 8 hours necrosis is largely irreversible. Nerve function fails earlier than muscle, which explains why early sensory change in the first web space is a useful sign in anterior compartment syndrome.

**Thresholds and controversy.** Early criteria used an absolute pressure above about 30 mmHg. McQueen and Court-Brown (1996) introduced the **perfusion pressure** threshold, ΔP = diastolic BP − compartment pressure, with fasciotomy indicated at below 30 mmHg. They showed this reduced unnecessary fasciotomies in tibial fractures. Later work questioned the specificity of a single ΔP reading, because transient low values are common and do not always mean the limb is failing. Pressure readings also vary with distance from the fracture, so the catheter should sit within about 5 cm of the fracture site.

**Fascial anatomy that matters.** The deep posterior compartment is the one most often missed. In some limbs tibialis posterior sits in its own fascial sheath, which can behave like a fifth compartment. Release therefore requires opening the deep fascia off the soleus bridge from a medial approach. The superficial fibular nerve pierces the crural fascia about 10–12 cm above the lateral malleolus, close to the lateral septum.

**Exertional compartment syndrome.** Chronic exertional compartment syndrome is a reversible, exercise-induced pressure rise, usually in the anterior or lateral compartments. Muscle volume increases by up to about 20% during exercise, and in a stiff fascial box this produces painful ischemia. The Pedowitz criteria for diagnosis are a pre-exercise pressure of at least 15 mmHg, a 1-minute post-exercise pressure of at least 30 mmHg, or a 5-minute post-exercise pressure of at least 20 mmHg. These criteria have been criticized for overlapping with readings from people without symptoms.
levels.expert:
**Fasciotomy technique.** The standard two-incision method uses an anterolateral incision for the anterior and lateral compartments and a medial incision for both posterior compartments.
- **Anterolateral incision.** It is placed about halfway between the tibial crest and the fibula. Before releasing the fascia, identify the intermuscular septum and the superficial fibular nerve.
- **Medial incision.** It is placed about 2 cm posterior to the tibial border to protect the saphenous vein and nerve. Take the soleus off the tibia to open the deep posterior compartment, and check that the flexor digitorum longus is fully released.

The single-incision perifibular approach can open all four compartments, but the deep posterior release is technically harder through it. Wounds are left open. They are later closed by delayed primary closure, shoelace techniques, negative-pressure dressings or skin grafting.

**Diagnostic pitfalls.** Clinical signs are least reliable in exactly the patients at highest risk:
- obtunded, intubated or polytrauma patients;
- children, where the "3 A's" (anxiety, agitation and an increasing need for analgesia) can be more useful than the classic "5 P's";
- patients with regional anesthesia or nerve blocks, where an ischemic limb may not feel painful.

In these groups, continuous pressure monitoring should be considered. Do not wait for loss of pulses; by that point the muscle has often already died.

**Consequences of a missed diagnosis.** A missed compartment syndrome can cause **Volkmann-type ischemic contracture**: claw toes, an equinus (fixed pointed-foot) deformity, and a chronically painful, numb foot. A late fasciotomy, done after the muscle is already dead, can turn a closed injury into an infected open wound. It may also trigger rhabdomyolysis-related kidney injury and hyperkalemia. For established late cases, many surgeons therefore advise against fasciotomy.

**New diagnostic approaches.** Researchers are studying near-infrared spectroscopy, which measures tissue oxygen saturation without needles. Others are testing intramuscular pH and glucose sensors, which may be more specific than pressure readings. Biomarker panels are also being explored. None of these has yet replaced clinical assessment combined with pressure measurement.

**Exertional syndrome treatment.** For chronic exertional compartment syndrome, gait retraining (moving from a heel strike to a forefoot strike) can reduce anterior compartment pressure and may avoid the need for surgery. For example, Diebal and colleagues reported this in military runners. If surgery is still needed, it is a fasciotomy, which can be done endoscopically. Recurrence and nerve injury occur at nontrivial rates.

**Open questions.** Should the decision to operate rely on a fixed ΔP threshold, on trends over time, or on metabolic markers? How should the threshold change for patients with low blood pressure? These remain unresolved.

keyPoints: Fascial septa and the interosseous membrane divide the leg into anterior, lateral and posterior (superficial and deep) compartments
Anterior compartment: dorsiflexors, deep fibular nerve, anterior tibial artery
Lateral compartment: fibularis longus and brevis evert the foot, supplied by the superficial fibular nerve
Posterior compartment: plantarflexors and inverters, tibial nerve, posterior tibial and fibular arteries
Common fibular nerve injury at the fibular neck causes foot drop
Compartment syndrome: pain on passive stretch, perfusion pressure below 30 mmHg, treated by fasciotomy

A Pedowitz test is needed before deciding

The superficial fibular nerve runs in the anterior compartment

Nerve tissue becomes ischemic before muscle does

lessons.title: Ankle, Subtalar & Midfoot Joints

levels.kid:
Your foot is not one stiff block. It is like a team of small bones held together with strong straps called ligaments.

The **ankle** is where your leg bones grab the top of a foot bone called the **talus**, a bit like a hand gripping a doorknob. It lets your toes point up and down, like pressing a car pedal.

Just below it is the **subtalar joint**. It lets your foot tilt in and out, so you can walk on bumpy grass or rocks without falling.

Further forward, the middle of your foot has more joints. They let the foot be soft and bendy when it lands, then firm like a lever when you push off. That is how one foot can be both a cushion and a springboard!
levels.hs:
The ankle and foot contain several joints that work together.

- The **talocrural joint** (true ankle) is a **hinge joint**. The **tibia** and **fibula** form a socket called the **mortise**, which grips the dome of the **talus**. It allows **dorsiflexion** (toes up) and **plantarflexion** (toes down). The bony bumps on each side are the **medial malleolus** (tibia) and **lateral malleolus** (fibula).
- The **subtalar joint**, between the talus and the **calcaneus** (heel bone), allows **inversion** (sole turns inward) and **eversion** (sole turns outward).
- The **midfoot** joints, including the **transverse tarsal joint** and the **tarsometatarsal (Lisfranc) joints**, fine-tune the foot's shape.

Ligaments hold it all together. On the outside, the **lateral ligaments** include the **anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL)**, the **calcaneofibular ligament** and the **posterior talofibular ligament**. On the inside, the thick, fan-shaped **deltoid ligament** is much stronger.

Real example: the common "rolled ankle" happens when the foot inverts while pointed down. This usually tears the ATFL first, because it is the weakest lateral ligament and is under the most tension in that position. That is why most ankle sprains hurt on the outside of the ankle.
levels.college:
**Talocrural joint.** This synovial hinge links the distal tibia (plafond and medial malleolus) and the fibula (lateral malleolus) to the trochlea of the talus. The trochlea is **wider anteriorly**, so the joint is most stable in dorsiflexion, when the wide part wedges into the mortise. In plantarflexion the narrow posterior trochlea allows some wobble, which is why sprains happen in plantarflexion plus inversion. The lateral malleolus extends further distally than the medial malleolus, which limits eversion.

The mortise is held together by the **distal tibiofibular syndesmosis**: the anterior and posterior inferior tibiofibular ligaments, the interosseous ligament and the inferior transverse ligament.

**Collateral ligaments:**
- **Lateral complex**: ATFL (most often injured), calcaneofibular ligament (CFL, crosses both the ankle and subtalar joints), and posterior talofibular ligament (strongest, rarely torn alone).
- **Medial (deltoid) ligament**: tibionavicular, tibiocalcaneal and anterior and posterior tibiotalar parts. It is so strong that forceful eversion often breaks off the medial malleolus instead of tearing the ligament.

**Subtalar joint.** The talus sits on the calcaneus at posterior, middle and anterior facets. The **interosseous talocalcaneal ligament** lies in the **tarsal sinus/canal** between them. Its oblique axis produces inversion and eversion. Combined with forefoot motion, these form **supination** and **pronation**.

**Transverse tarsal (Chopart) joint.** This combines the talonavicular and calcaneocuboid joints. The **spring (plantar calcaneonavicular) ligament** supports the head of the talus.

**Tarsometatarsal (Lisfranc) joints.** The base of the 2nd metatarsal is recessed between the cuneiforms like a keystone. The **Lisfranc ligament** runs from the medial cuneiform to the 2nd metatarsal base. There is no ligament linking the 1st and 2nd metatarsal bases.

Nerve supply follows Hilton's law: the deep fibular, tibial and sural nerves supply the ankle.
levels.phd:
**Ankle kinematics.** The talocrural axis is not purely transverse. It runs roughly through the malleolar tips, angled downward laterally and posteriorly. So dorsiflexion is coupled with slight abduction, and plantarflexion with adduction. Inman's classic work described the trochlea as a section of a cone, not a cylinder, with its apex directed medially. This explains the rotational coupling and why fibular position matters for congruence. During dorsiflexion the wider anterior talus pushes the fibula laterally and rotates it, and the syndesmosis allows small movements of about a millimetre or so. That is why the joint is often described as a mortise that is slightly flexible rather than rigid.

Contact mechanics show that the tibiotalar joint carries very large loads, several times body weight in late stance, across a relatively small contact area. Lateral talar shift reduces that area sharply. Ramsey and Hamilton's classic cadaver study reported that a 1 mm lateral shift cut contact area by about 42%. This finding underpins the low tolerance for malreduction in fractures.

**Subtalar and transverse tarsal coupling.** The subtalar axis (Manter, Inman) is inclined about 42 degrees from the horizontal and about 23 degrees medial to the long axis of the foot, acting like a mitered hinge. Leg internal rotation drives eversion (pronation), and external rotation drives inversion. This links tibial rotation to foot posture. Elftman proposed that the talonavicular and calcaneocuboid axes are parallel when the calcaneus is everted, which unlocks the midfoot so it adapts during loading response. Inversion makes the axes converge and locks the midfoot into a rigid lever for push-off. Later 3D studies question the simple locking model, but the functional idea of coupling still holds.

**Ligament material properties.** The ATFL has the lowest load to failure of the lateral ligaments. The CFL tolerates more strain and the PTFL is strongest, matching the sequential tear pattern (ATFL, then CFL, then PTFL) seen in inversion injuries. In the deltoid complex, the deep tibiotalar fibres are the main restraint to lateral talar shift. Their integrity separates stable from unstable lateral malleolar fractures.

**Midfoot.** The recessed 2nd metatarsal and the dorsal-to-plantar trapezoidal shapes of the bases form a Roman-arch keystone. The interosseous Lisfranc ligament is the strongest part of that complex.
levels.expert:
**Imaging and classification.** Ankle radiographs are often guided by the **Ottawa ankle rules**: tenderness at the posterior edge or tip of either malleolus, or inability to bear weight, prompts imaging. On the mortise view, a **medial clear space** wider than the superior clear space (often quoted as more than 4 to 5 mm) implies deltoid incompetence. **Tibiofibular clear space** widening implies syndesmotic injury. The **Lauge-Hansen** (foot position plus force direction) and **Weber** (fibular fracture level relative to the syndesmosis: A below, B at, C above) schemes guide decisions. A **Maisonneuve** injury, a proximal fibular fracture with syndesmotic and medial disruption, is a classic miss if the knee is not examined. The proximal fibular neck is close to the common fibular nerve, a detail worth noting for neurosurgery-minded readers.

**Syndesmosis fixation.** Fixation with screws versus suture-button devices remains debated. Suture-buttons allow physiological micromotion and lower rates of malreduction and removal. Weight-bearing CT and intraoperative 3D imaging are increasingly used, because malreduction on plain films is underdetected.

**Chronic lateral instability.** About a fifth to a third of sprains leave residual symptoms. Anatomical repair (the **Brostrom-Gould** procedure, reinforced with the extensor retinaculum) is standard. All-arthroscopic repair and synthetic tape augmentation are expanding. Concurrent problems to look for include osteochondral lesions of the talar dome, peroneal tendon tears, and subtalar instability, which is difficult to separate clinically because the CFL bridges both joints.

**Lisfranc injuries.** About 20% are missed initially. Red flags include **plantar ecchymosis** in the midfoot and a "fleck sign" (avulsion near the 2nd metatarsal base). Weight-bearing or stress views help unmask subtle diastasis. For purely ligamentous injuries, primary arthrodesis may lead to fewer reoperations than open reduction and internal fixation, though the evidence is still debated.

**Chopart and subtalar.** Subtalar dislocations are usually medial. Lateral dislocations are higher-energy and often open. In **tarsal coalition** (calcaneonavicular or talocalcaneal), adolescents present with a rigid flatfoot and recurrent sprains, which is relevant to Odin's age group.

**Open questions** include the best fixation for the syndesmosis, whether total ankle arthroplasty can match arthrodesis durability in younger patients, and how to model 3D subtalar coupling for patient-specific implants.

keyPoints: Talocrural (true ankle) is a hinge: dorsiflexion and plantarflexion
Talar trochlea is wider in front, so the ankle is most stable in dorsiflexion
Inversion sprains tear the ATFL first, then the CFL
Deltoid ligament is strong; eversion often fractures the medial malleolus instead
Subtalar joint (talus-calcaneus) produces inversion and eversion
Lisfranc ligament links medial cuneiform to 2nd metatarsal base; injuries are often missed

lessons.title: Foot Arches, Plantar Layers & the Gait Cycle

levels.kid:
Look at the bottom of your foot. The middle part curves up and does not touch the floor. That curve is called an **arch**. It works like a bridge made of little bones.

The arch is a bit springy. When you land on your foot, it squishes down a tiny bit to soak up the bump. Then it springs back to help push you forward.

Under the arch are layers of small muscles and a tough strap called the **plantar fascia**. They hold the bridge up, like ropes on a bow.

Walking has a pattern. First your heel touches the ground. Then your whole foot is down. Then your toes push off, and your leg swings forward. Then it all happens again!
levels.hs:
The foot is not flat. Its bones form **arches** that make it both a shock absorber and a stiff lever for pushing off.

There are three arches:
- **Medial longitudinal arch**: the high inner arch, running from the heel bone (calcaneus) through the talus, navicular, three cuneiforms and first three metatarsals. Its keystone is the head of the talus.
- **Lateral longitudinal arch**: lower and flatter, through the calcaneus, cuboid and fourth and fifth metatarsals.
- **Transverse arch**: runs side to side across the cuneiforms, cuboid and metatarsal bases.

Arches are supported by bone shape, ligaments, the **plantar aponeurosis** (a thick band of connective tissue under the sole) and muscles. The sole has **four layers** of intrinsic muscles, stacked from the skin inward.

**Gait** is the walking pattern. One **gait cycle** runs from one heel strike to the next heel strike of the same foot. About 60% of the cycle is the **stance phase** (foot on the ground) and about 40% is the **swing phase** (foot in the air).

A real example: **flat foot (pes planus)**. In many children the arch looks flat until it develops with age. In adults, a common acquired cause is failure of the **tibialis posterior** tendon, which normally helps hold up the medial arch.
levels.college:
**Arch support** has three tiers: bony architecture, passive ligaments and dynamic muscle.
- Key ligaments of the medial arch: the **plantar calcaneonavicular (spring) ligament**, which cradles the talar head, plus the long and short plantar ligaments, which mainly support the lateral column.
- The **plantar aponeurosis** runs from the calcaneal tuberosity to the toes and acts like the tie-beam of a truss.
- Dynamic supports: **tibialis posterior** (medial arch), **fibularis longus** crossing the sole to the first metatarsal (transverse and medial arch), **flexor hallucis longus**, and the intrinsic muscles.

**Plantar layers** (superficial to deep):
- **Layer 1**: abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis, abductor digiti minimi.
- **Layer 2**: quadratus plantae and the lumbricals, plus the tendons of flexor digitorum longus and flexor hallucis longus.
- **Layer 3**: flexor hallucis brevis, adductor hallucis (oblique and transverse heads), flexor digiti minimi brevis.
- **Layer 4**: plantar and dorsal interossei, plus the tendons of tibialis posterior and fibularis longus.
Innervation: the **medial plantar nerve** supplies abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis, flexor hallucis brevis and the first lumbrical. The **lateral plantar nerve** supplies the rest. Both are branches of the tibial nerve.

**Windlass mechanism**: dorsiflexing the toes at push-off winds the plantar aponeurosis around the metatarsal heads. This shortens the foot, raises the arch, inverts the heel and turns the foot into a rigid lever.

**Gait cycle** (Rancho Los Amigos terms):
- Stance: initial contact, loading response, midstance, terminal stance, preswing.
- Swing: initial swing, midswing, terminal swing.
In walking, both feet are on the ground for two periods of **double support**. Running has no double support and adds a float phase. At loading response, the ankle dorsiflexors work eccentrically to lower the forefoot. In terminal stance, the gastrocnemius and soleus give the main push-off.
levels.phd:
The foot changes during each stance phase from a compliant adapter into a rigid lever. Two linked mechanisms do this. The first is **subtalar pronation**: eversion at heel strike unlocks the **transverse tarsal (Chopart) joint**. When it is unlocked, the axes of the talonavicular and calcaneocuboid joints are roughly parallel, so the midfoot is flexible. Supination in late stance makes these axes cross, which locks the midfoot.

The second is the **windlass mechanism**, described by **Hicks (1954)**. When the toes extend at the metatarsophalangeal joints, the plantar aponeurosis is pulled around the metatarsal heads like a cable on a drum. This raises the arch and supinates the hindfoot. Ker and colleagues (1987, *Nature*) showed that the arch also works as a **spring**. Ligaments and the aponeurosis store elastic strain energy in early stance and return part of it at push-off; the Achilles tendon stores even more. Kelly and colleagues have shown that the plantar intrinsic muscles are actively recruited as load rises. This supports an **active foot core** model rather than a purely passive truss.

Two questions remain debated:
- How much of arch stiffness comes from ligaments versus muscles. Nerve-block studies of the intrinsics show they matter, but less than the passive structures.
- Whether arch height predicts injury. Large prospective cohorts, including one in novice runners, did not find a strong link between foot posture and running injury risk.

The **midtarsal break**, a flexible midfoot that bends at the transverse tarsal joint, is present in chimpanzees and largely absent in humans. Its variable expression in modern humans and in hominin fossils such as the Laetoli footprints and *Australopithecus* feet informs debates on when bipedalism evolved.

In gait, the work done by the ankle in late stance is the largest source of positive power in walking. Perry's three **rockers** describe how the body moves forward over the foot: the heel rocker, the ankle rocker and the forefoot rocker.
levels.expert:
**Adult acquired flatfoot**, now called **progressive collapsing foot deformity (PCFD)** after a 2020 consensus, is more than tibialis posterior tendon failure. Attenuation of the spring ligament and the talocalcaneal interosseous ligament is often the key lesion. Clinical signs include the **"too many toes" sign** and an inability to do a single-leg heel rise with the heel swinging into inversion. Weight-bearing CT now allows the deformity to be mapped in 3D. A key question in planning surgery is whether the deformity is flexible or rigid. Flexible deformities may be treated with tendon transfer, often flexor digitorum longus, plus a medializing calcaneal osteotomy. Rigid deformities need arthrodesis.

**Pes cavus** matters to anyone heading for neurosurgery. A high arch often points to a neurologic cause, such as Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, a tethered cord, a spinal cord tumour or Friedreich ataxia. This is especially likely when the cavus is in one foot only or is getting worse. In CMT, a weak tibialis anterior and fibularis brevis are overpowered by fibularis longus and tibialis posterior. The result is a plantarflexed first ray and a hindfoot pushed into varus. The **Coleman block test** shows whether the hindfoot varus is driven by the forefoot. A new cavus foot should prompt a neurologic exam and imaging of the spine.

The **plantar fascia** is a common source of pain. In **plantar fasciitis**, which is degenerative (fasciosis) rather than truly inflammatory, the fascia is typically thicker than 4 mm on ultrasound. Pain from entrapment of **Baxter's nerve**, the first branch of the lateral plantar nerve, between abductor hallucis and quadratus plantae, is often mistaken for plantar fasciitis. Tarsal tunnel syndrome is another look-alike.

In gait labs, footdrop shows up as a **steppage gait**, in which the hip and knee lift high so the toes clear the ground during swing. A gluteus medius lesion produces a **Trendelenburg gait** instead. Recent advances include instrumented insoles, markerless video motion capture and intrinsic-foot strengthening programmes. The last are supported by early randomized trials but are not yet definitive.

keyPoints: Three arches: medial longitudinal, lateral longitudinal and transverse
The talar head is the keystone of the medial arch, cradled by the spring ligament
The sole has four muscle layers, supplied by the medial and lateral plantar nerves
The windlass mechanism stiffens the arch when the toes dorsiflex at push-off
Gait cycle: stance about 60%, swing about 40%; walking has double support, running has a float phase
A new or one-sided pes cavus can signal neurologic disease such as CMT

test.q: Which bone is the keystone of the medial longitudinal arch?
test.explain: The talar head sits at the top of the medial arch and is cradled by the spring ligament. The cuboid belongs to the lateral column.

test.q: The spring ligament runs between which two bones?
test.explain: The plantar calcaneonavicular (spring) ligament supports the talar head from below.

test.q: Which muscle lies in the first plantar layer?
test.explain: Layer 1 contains abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis and abductor digiti minimi. Quadratus plantae is in layer 2.

test.q: Which muscle does the medial plantar nerve supply?
test.explain: The medial plantar nerve supplies abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis, flexor hallucis brevis and the first lumbrical. The lateral plantar nerve supplies the others listed.

test.q: What does the windlass mechanism do when the toes dorsiflex?
choices: Raises the arch and stiffens the foot
Lowers the arch for shock absorption
Everts the heel to unlock the midfoot
test.explain: Toe extension winds the aponeurosis around the metatarsal heads. This raises the arch and makes the foot a rigid lever.

test.q: About what share of the walking gait cycle is stance phase?
test.explain: Stance is about 60% of the cycle and swing about 40%.

test.q: Running differs from walking because running has:
test.explain: In running, double support disappears and both feet are off the ground for a moment during the float phase.

test.q: A common acquired cause of adult flat foot is failure of which tendon?
test.explain: Tibialis posterior is a key dynamic support of the medial arch. Its failure is a classic cause of adult flat foot.

test.q: Which bones form the lateral longitudinal arch?
test.explain: The lower lateral arch runs through the calcaneus, cuboid and the fourth and fifth metatarsals.

test.q: What is the medical name for flat foot? (pes ___)
test.explain: Pes planus means flat foot. Pes cavus means high arch.

test.q: The thick band under the sole that acts as the tie-beam of the arch is the plantar ___.
test.explain: The plantar aponeurosis, also called the plantar fascia, runs from the calcaneus to the toes.

test.q: Which nerve gives off the medial and lateral plantar nerves?
test.explain: The tibial nerve divides into the medial and lateral plantar nerves.

kidTest.q: What is the curve under the middle of your foot called?
kidTest.explain: The curved part under your foot is the arch.

kidTest.q: What does the springy arch do when you land?
kidTest.explain: The arch squishes a little to cushion each step.

kidTest.q: Which part of your foot usually touches the ground first when you walk?
kidTest.explain: Walking starts with the heel touching down.

kidTest.q: What helps hold the arch up?
choices: The hard toenails on your toes
The thin skin on top of your foot
kidTest.explain: Small muscles and a tough strap called the plantar fascia hold the arch up, like ropes on a bow.

kidTest.q: The arch is built like a b _ _ _ _ _ made of little bones.
kidTest.explain: Like a bridge, the arch is strong and curved.

advancedTest.q: Why is the midfoot flexible at heel strike but rigid at push-off?
choices: Chopart joint axes are parallel in pronation and cross in supination
The talus moves away from the navicular as the foot pronates
Plantar interossei shorten the transverse arch during swing
The spring ligament contracts actively during late stance
advancedTest.explain: Pronation makes the transverse tarsal joint axes parallel, so the midfoot is mobile. Supination makes them cross, which locks it. The spring ligament is passive and cannot contract.

advancedTest.q: A teenager has a new high arch in one foot only. What is the most appropriate next step?
choices: Give reassurance, as this is a normal variant
Do a neurologic exam and image the spine
Do a plantar fascia release straight away
Fit custom orthotics and review in a year
advancedTest.explain: A new or one-sided pes cavus suggests a neurologic cause such as a tethered cord, a spinal tumour or CMT. It needs a neurologic workup.

advancedTest.q: In Charcot-Marie-Tooth cavus, a plantarflexed first ray mainly comes from:
choices: Weak tibialis anterior and a strong fibularis longus
A tight spring ligament pulling up on the talus
Weak tibialis posterior and a strong tibialis anterior
Overactive lumbricals flexing the first toe
advancedTest.explain: Fibularis longus inserts on the first metatarsal. When it is unopposed by a weak tibialis anterior, it pulls the first ray down.

advancedTest.q: Heel pain that persists after treatment for plantar fasciitis, with a burning quality, should raise suspicion of:
choices: Rupture of the long plantar ligament
Injury to the deep fibular nerve
advancedTest.explain: Entrapment of Baxter's nerve, the first branch of the lateral plantar nerve, between abductor hallucis and quadratus plantae causes burning heel pain that is often mistaken for plantar fasciitis.
